## Description {#details}

A class template for the intrusive list iterator.

<ParametersList title="Template Parameters">
<ParametersListItem name="T">Type of object that includes the intrusive node.</ParametersListItem>
<ParametersListItem name="N">Type of intrusive node. Must have the public members <b>previous</b> &amp; <b>next</b>.</ParametersListItem>
<ParametersListItem name="MP">Name of the intrusive node member in object T.</ParametersListItem>
<ParametersListItem name="U">Type stored in the list, derived from T.</ParametersListItem>
</ParametersList>
This class provides an interface similar to <code>std::list::iterator</code>, except that it keeps track of the offset where the intrusive list element is located in the parent object. It supports bidirectional iteration and access to the underlying object and node.

### intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator() {#a93cc9e0b0cc3629edb655faec0feb4b3}

<MemberDefinition

  labels = {["constexpr"]}>
Default constructor. Constructs an iterator pointing to <code>nullptr</code>.

The default constructor for <code><Link to="/docs/api/classes/micro-os-plus/utils/intrusive-list-iterator">intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator</Link></code> initialises the iterator to a null state, meaning it does not point to any node in the list. This is typically used to create an &quot;end&quot; iterator or to initialise an iterator variable before assigning it to a valid node.


:::info
The internal node pointer is value-initialised (set to <code>nullptr</code>), ensuring that the iterator is safe to use in comparisons and will not dereference an invalid address.
:::

### get&#95;pointer() {#a11f2bc99a1f478650b82546e2e5470d1}

<MemberDefinition
  template={<>template &lt;class T, class N, N T::&#42; MP, class U = T&gt;</>}
  prototype={<>intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator&lt; T, N, MP, U &gt;::pointer micro&#95;os&#95;plus::utils::intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator&lt; T, N, MP, U &gt;::get&#95;pointer (void) const</>}
  labels = {["inline"]}>
Get the object node from the intrusive node.

<SectionUser title="Parameters">
None.
</SectionUser>


<SectionUser title="Returns">
Pointer to object node.
</SectionUser>

Computes and returns a pointer to the parent object that contains the intrusive node currently referenced by the iterator. This is achieved by calculating the offset of the intrusive node member within the parent object type and subtracting it from the node&#39;s address. This technique allows the iterator to provide access to the full object from just the node pointer, enabling intrusive list traversal and manipulation.

### operator!=() {#aa5703a48802f7fa6c20df08a5d90a3fa}

<MemberDefinition

<ParametersList title="Parameters">
<ParametersListItem name="other">Iterator to compare with.</ParametersListItem>
</ParametersList>

<SectionUser title="Returns">
<code>true</code> if the iterators point to different nodes, <code>false</code> otherwise.
</SectionUser>

The inequality comparison operator (<code>operator!=</code>) checks whether two intrusive list iterators point to different nodes in the list by comparing their internal node pointers. This is useful for standard iterator operations, such as determining whether an iterator has reached the end of a range or for loop termination conditions.

### operator&#42;() {#a5db55a56e22dbdea96e6d7e05c52f4c8}

<MemberDefinition
  template={<>template &lt;class T, class N, N T::&#42; MP, class U = T&gt;</>}
  prototype={<>intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator&lt; T, N, MP, U &gt;::reference micro&#95;os&#95;plus::utils::intrusive&#95;list&#95;iterator&lt; T, N, MP, U &gt;::operator&#42; () const</>}
  labels = {["inline"]}>
Dereference operator.

<SectionUser title="Returns">
Reference to the value pointed to by the iterator.
</SectionUser>

The dereference operator (<code>operator&#42;</code>) provides access to the value or object pointed to by the iterator. Internally, it calls <code><Link to="#a11f2bc99a1f478650b82546e2e5470d1">get&#95;pointer()</Link></code> to obtain a pointer to the underlying value or object associated with the current node in the list, and then dereferences it to return a reference.

This allows the iterator to be used in a manner similar to standard C++ iterators, enabling direct access to the list element for reading or modification.
